title: Antonio-Perez, Luis, Crime Victim Order
text:
62 Van Natta 594 (2010) 594
In the Matter of the Compensation of
LUIS ANTONIO-PEREZ, Claimant
WCB Case No. 09-00002CV
ORDER ON RECONSIDERATION (CRIME VICTIMS ACT)
Law Office Of Erin Olson PC, Claimant Attorneys
Robert W Connell, Dept Of Justice
Reviewing Panel: Members Biehl and Lowell.
On February 11, 2010, Special Hearing Officer Debra L. Young issued
Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law and Opinion, and a Proposed Order that
dismissed Applicant’s request for relief under the Crime Victims’ Act,
ORS Chapter 147, for lack of jurisdiction and returned the matter to the
Department of Justice for an Order on Reconsideration. Specifically, the Hearings
Officer: (1) determined that the Board’s jurisdiction is not limited to appeals of
compensability decisions rendered by the Department of Justice and may include
issues regarding the amount of compensation; and (2) dismissed the Applicant’s
request for relief because the Department had not issued any decision regarding
the amount of compensation.1
We agree with the Hearing Officer's reasoning and conclusions regarding the
issue of whether the Board has jurisdiction over issues concerning the amount of
compensation. However, we conclude that a further order from the Department is
unnecessary.
FINDINGS OF FACT
We adopt the Hearing Officer’s “Findings of Fact.”
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW AND OPINION
We briefly summarize the factual background of the claim. On October 24,
2008, Applicant sustained severe injuries after an assault. After he applied for
crime victim compensation benefits, the Department issued a Determination Order
on February 9, 2009 that denied such benefits. (Ex. 3B).
1 We have received objections from the Department. Nevertheless, because those objections
were mailed to the Board on March 4 (21 days from the Hearing Officer’s order), they are untimely filed.
OAR 438-082-0040; OAR 438-005-0046. Consequently, the Department’s objections have hot been
considered and we have proceeded with our reconsideration on our own motion.

62 Van Natta 594 (2010) 595
On February 22, 2009, Applicant’s attorney appealed that Determination
Order. (Ex. 3C-1). On April 14, 2009, the attorney clarified that Applicant was
requesting a “re-review of [the Department’s] denial.” (Ex. 2C-1).
The Department issued a Determination Order on April 23, 2009, which
concluded that Applicant was the victim of a compensable crime and met all
eligibility criteria under ORS 147.015. The order stated that “eligibility for
compensation under ORS 147.005 to 147.365 is met” and that the Department
“will pay for those expenses that are compensable losses.” (Ex. 2B).
Applicant’s medical expenses exceeded $80,000. (Exs. 1D through 47D).
The Department, however, paid for only $20,000 of those medical expenses.
(Ex. 48D). Contending that ORS 147.035(2) provided a maximum of $44,000 in
damages, Applicant’s attorney requested that the Department pay an additional
$24,000 toward medical expenses.
In response, the Department asserted that there was a $20,000 statutory
maximum on an individual victim’s compensable expenses. (Ex. 4C). The
Department did not issue an order regarding applicant’s request. Applicant then
requested a hearing by the Workers’ Compensation Board (Board) regarding the
Department’s refusal to pay an additional $24,000 in medical expenses.
In concluding that the Board is authorized to review a challenge to the
amount of crime victim compensation, the Hearing Officer explained that if an
Applicant disagrees with the Department’s order under ORS 147.135, he/she may
request review by the Department pursuant to ORS 147.145. Thereafter, the
Department “shall reconsider” any order for which a request is received. Under
ORS 147.155, it is not until an Applicant disagrees with the Department’s
reconsideration order issued under ORS 147.145 that the Applicant may appeal
to the Board.
The Hearing Officer then concluded that the context of the statutory review
procedures after the Department’s initial order likewise do not limit the issue to
compensability. In other words, according to the Hearings Officer, if the initial
order is not limited to compensability issues, review of that initial order either by
the Department under ORS 147.145 or the Board’s subsequent review under
ORS 147.155 is also not limited to compensability issues.
Accordingly, based on the above reasoning, the Hearing Officer
determined that the Board’s jurisdiction in this matter was not limited to appeals
of compensability decisions and may include issues regarding the amount of

62 Van Natta 594 (2010) 596
compensation. Nevertheless, the Hearing Officer concluded that the Department’s
orders did not determine the amount of compensation for which Applicant had
been found eligible as a crime victim. Rather, the Officer reasoned that the dispute
concerning the amount of Applicant’s compensation did not arise until after the
Department’s April 2009 order, when he was advised of the Department’s
intention to limit payment to his medical providers to $20,000 and contended that
he was entitled to a maximum of $44,000 under ORS 147.035(2)(b).
According to the Hearing Officer, the amount of compensation issue was a
different matter from the compensability issue decided by the Department’s April
2009 order. Moreover, the Officer reasoned that the Department had not issued
any written decision regarding this new issue. As such, the Hearing Officer
concluded that, because the Department remained responsible to issue a decision
under ORS 147.135, the monetary dispute was not in the Board’s jurisdiction.
Consequently, the Hearing Officer returned the case to the Department for
issuance of an Order on Reconsideration.
While we agree with and adopt the Hearings Officer’s analysis of the
relevant statutory provisions and conclusion regarding the Board’s authority to
review issues regarding the amount of compensation due under the Act, we
disagree with her decision to dismiss Applicant’s request for relief. We reason
as follows.
The Hearing Officer concluded that, because there was no reconsideration
order from the Department, the issue regarding the amount of compensation was
not properly before the Board. Yet, the Department has, in effect, issued a
reconsideration order. The first Department order (issued on February 2, 2009)
denied the application for benefits. However, after receiving additional
information from Applicant’s counsel, the Department issued a second order on
April 23, 2009, finding the claim compensable and awarding compensation.
Under such circumstances, we conclude that the Department, in essence,
issued a “reconsideration” order; i.e., it reconsidered its February 2, 2009 order
denying benefits, found the claim compensable, and awarded benefits. In
response, Applicant has contested that order, challenging the amount of
compensation arising from that decision.2 Because there is no time limit on
2 Because the Department’s order awarded compensation and Applicant has requested Board
review seeking an increased award, we believe that Applicant’s intention is clear and unambiguous:
he disagrees with the Department’s interpretation of its April 2009 decision awarding compensation.

62 Van Natta 594 (2010) 597
requesting review of a Department’s reconsideration order and because the
Department’s second order awarded compensation, Applicant’s objection to the
“amount” of compensation awarded by the Department is before the Board.3
See Patricia A. Williams, 52 Van Natta 38, 38 (2000) (finding no specific time
limitation on an appeal of an Order on Reconsideration issued by the Department
under ORS 147.145).
Consequently, the Department is not required to issue another order
addressing the amount of compensation and applicant is not required to request
another hearing. Instead, because Applicant has already requested review of a
reconsideration order, it is unnecessary to return this matter to the Department for
another order.
Finally, in order to give the parties a final opportunity to supplement their
respective arguments regarding the substantive issue (whether Applicant is entitled
to compensation in the amount of $20,000, as found by the Department, or in the
amount of $44,000, as argued by Applicant), we implement the following briefing
schedule: Applicant’s opening supplemental brief is due 21 days from the date of
this order. The Department's supplemental response is due within 21 days from the
date of mailing of Applicant’s brief. Applicant’s reply is due 14 days from the
date of mailing of the Department’s response. Thereafter, we shall take the
“amount” of compensation issue under advisement.4
IT IS SO ORDERED
Entered at Salem, Oregon on March 10, 2010
3 We decline to interpret the Department’s actions in a manner that would require it to simply
issue another order which would merely reiterate its current position regarding Applicant’s request
(except that the order would be entitled “Order on Reconsideration”) and then require Applicant to re-file
a request for Board review, seeking exactly the same relief that he presently requests.
4 The parties may wish to consider using the Board’s mediation services, which are offered free
of charge. If the parties are willing to participate in mediation, they can notify the Board’s executive
secretary, Karen Burton, at 503-934-0123. Thereafter, the briefing schedule/Board review would be
suspended.
